d: The band of cervix between the original and the new squamocolumnar junction, where columnar epithelium has turned squamous by metaplasia. Its immature cells are the target of high-risk HPV.
A harmless mucus-filled bump on the cervix. It forms when squamous metaplasia covers the opening of an endocervical gland and traps its mucus. It needs no treatment.
A squamous cell changed by HPV, with an enlarged, wrinkled, dark (raisinoid) nucleus and a clear halo around it. It is typical of LSIL and of genital warts.
Strong, continuous p16 staining across the epithelium. It happens because E7 inactivates Rb, and it points to an HPV-driven high-grade lesion (HSIL).
Magnified examination of the cervix after acetic acid, which turns abnormal areas white so they can be biopsied. It is the diagnostic step after an abnormal screening result.
Removal of the transformation zone with a thin wire loop carrying electric current, used to treat high-grade lesions (HSIL). Like any cone excision, it can later cause cervical insufficiency.
The standard way to report Pap results. It says whether the sample is adequate, then gives a category such as NILM, ASC-US, LSIL, HSIL, atypical glandular cells or carcinoma.

Outward turning of the columnar endocervical lining onto the ectocervix, seen as a red, velvety ring around the opening. It is benign and common with high estrogen, and it can cause mucoid discharge and contact bleeding.
